story_text.value:
Hi

We built [Mintly](https://usemintly.com) to make ad creation stupid simple. You pick an ad layout from brands like Gymshark or rhode, upload your product image, and it recreates the ad with your colors, logo, and product — no design skills needed.

I kinda got annoyed with how complicated or sucky some of these tools were + I live by two philosophies: keep it simple and steal what works. So we automated the entire process. Mintly now gets used by 500+ brands, and it takes ~60 seconds to go from product image → finished ad.

Would love to hear your feedback, questions, or suggestions. Happy to share how we built it, how we source top ad layouts, and what worked/didn’t work along the way.

comment_text.value:
Author here. We sell a $49 one-time kit that generates the three files agents read (agents.json, llms.txt, agent-instructions.md). This MCP server is the check — free, read-only — point your assistant at it and ask about any store.

Two honest limits up front: (1) agents.json is an emerging convention, not a ratified standard; we bet on the category (declared action affordances), not the filename — if a better standard wins, the kit ships it. (2) simulate_agent_shopping is a reasoned assessment from the site's exposed signals, not a literal checkout — no orders are placed.

What surprised us: sites with llms.txt but no agents.json (gymshark 21/100, allbirds 30/100) — the agent can read the catalog but completes 0–1 of 5 shopper tasks. Reading ≠ acting. Curious whether that matches what people see pointing their own agents at their sites.

story_title.value: An MCP tool that lets ChatGPT check if a store is AI-readable

crossfit made the gym (and free weights) cool

crossfit became popular as a side effect of "bootcamp" style workouts in the 2000s-2010s, like the Spartan Run, Tough Mudder, Rucking, etc.

mark rippetoe, creator of Starting Strength, was heavily involved in crossfit. between that and him franchising his Starting Strength practice, powerlifting became more widely practiced. once Instagram started building lifestyle brands around this (gymshark, alphalete, nobull, darcsport, etc.), it was a lock.

comment_text.value:
I was curious about how the creator economy actually works, not the influencer marketing pitch decks, but the actual structure.

- Who mentions who in their videos?

- Which brands keep showing up across the same creators?

So I built a pipeline that analyzes YouTube videos at scale, extracts every person mentioned and every brand sponsor, and builds a relationship graph from it. No manual data entry. Everything is extracted from what creators actually say and show.

Current data: 32K creators, 55K relationship edges, 2,700 brands. Started deep in fitness and gaming YouTube.

Things to try out:

- Search "Gymshark". See their sponsored creators, which categories they target, and which brands compete for the same roster

- Search "MrBeast". See his connection network

- Click a category tab on the homepage to filter both creators and brands

The hardest technical problem was entity resolution. The same person gets mentioned as "Jeff Nippard", "Jeff", "Nippard" across thousands of videos. Getting that right is what makes the graph useful.

Stack: FastAPI, Next.js, PostgreSQL, Fly.io. Gemini 2.0 Flash for structured extraction.

No signup, no paywall.

story_title.value: Show HN: Creatomap: Search who knows who and who pays who on YouTube

comment_text.value:
Ever noticed how ChatGPT gets brand info wrong — like reviews, pricing, or even what’s currently in stock?

We tested this across a bunch of e-commerce brands. For Gymshark, ChatGPT was consistently wrong about what’s in their “Best Sellers” or “New Arrivals.” For Glossier, it completely missed the Mother’s Day promo that’s live on their homepage right now.

Reviews are another weak spot. When someone asks “What are some reviews for Brand X?”, ChatGPT rarely shows real quotes or trusted sources. It pulls from all over — often outdated or off-brand. But because that info is scattered across the web, we realized you can guide ChatGPT to emphasize the content you actually want surfaced: the 5-star reviews, the UGC with quotes, the pages that convert.

We built something that does exactly that — it keeps ChatGPT aligned with the content that matters to your brand, in real time. So whether someone asks for reviews, current deals, or “best-selling colognes on Scentbird,” the right answers show up.

You also don't have to change your website root directory at all (r any other server side changes). We do ask you to put some tags (like analytics tags) in your client side code so we can monitor traffic & impact. If you're interested visit the website. Would love to also hear some ideas/things you've come across in this space.

story_title.value: Change What ChatGPT says about you
